Tonkawa

The Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma is a contemporary sovereign community. The Tribe’s public history centers the 1884–1885 forced removal from Fort Griffin, Texas, to Oakland in present-day Oklahoma. Historical records describe Tonkawa-speaking communities and named groups across Texas and the southern plains, but their composition, earlier locations, and relationships remain debated. This guide puts the Tribe’s present account beside archival and scholarly records, including a treaty, federal reports, and a later Tonkawa memorial challenging a land cession.

A source guide for a deeper dive.This entry provides a brief orientation and an organized reading path. A comprehensive deep dive has not yet been completed. Follow the annotated sources and distinguish primary community accounts from outside reference material.
Still unfinished

Seven substantive inspected works now support a stronger initial guide: the Tribe’s public history and language resource, TxDOT’s 2021 historical synthesis, Jones’s 1969 Smithsonian study, the 1837 Texas treaty, the 1891 federal agreement record, and a council-adopted Tonkawa memorial with member affidavits. Six supporting access/context references remain excluded. The primary records significantly improve the legal and land history, including a documented disagreement about the 1891 cession, but this is still an early source guide. It does not establish consent, resolve the later claim, or provide a deep account of every Tonkawa community and period.

Assessment recorded October 23, 2026. This is separate from research completion and community review.

01

A contemporary Tribe and the scope of this entry

The Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma’s public profile places its headquarters and community in Kay County and describes an elected Tribal Committee and a constitution adopted in 1938 with amendments listed through 2014. The same undated page lists population, enrollment, and acreage totals; those figures are omitted as current statistics. This entry centers the present-day Tribe while examining older Tonkawa and Tonkawa-associated names as historical records use them.

Read the sources [4] Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma [1] Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma [12] Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma; printed by the U.S. Senate in the Congressional Serial Set

02

Names and language

The Tribe’s public history gives “Tickanwa-tic” as its self-name and identifies “Tonkaweya” as a Waco/Wichita name. Spellings in older records vary. Don Paterson’s introductory language outline was prepared for the Tribe’s language-restoration program; it includes a pronunciation guide and a first lesson, and explains its intended learning context. It documents a public educational resource, not the current reach of language programs or a count of speakers.

Read the sources [1] Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma [7] Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma, Language Restoration and Preservation Program Series [9] Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma [6] Smithsonian Institution, Smithsonian Contributions to Anthropology 2(5)

03

Texas histories and changing geography

TxDOT’s 2021 report follows references from the seventeenth century through the nineteenth, including mission activity around the San Xavier/San Gabriel rivers and later locations across central Texas. Jones’s 1969 Smithsonian study assembles older colonial and American accounts. These records are uneven and mediated; their named bands and locations do not form a precise boundary map. TxDOT describes the statewide project as collaborative with participating Tribes, but this specific Tonkawa report does not identify a Tribal reviewer or approval.

Read the sources [5] Texas Department of Transportation [6] Smithsonian Institution, Smithsonian Contributions to Anthropology 2(5) [8] Texas State Historical Association

04

Diplomacy and written agreements

A November 1837 treaty records terms negotiated by Tonkawa head chiefs and a Republic of Texas commissioner, including mutual peace language and a Republic-appointed trading agent. A separate 1846 multination treaty catalogue lists Longwha (Tonkawa) among the parties at Council Springs; this review has not inspected the treaty text itself. These documents show what governments recorded and how the Tonkawa were named in particular proceedings, but they do not establish later implementation or a single Tonkawa view of every agreement.

Read the sources [11] Texas State Library and Archives Commission / Texas History Trust digital edition [13] National Archives and Records Administration and Indigenous Digital Archive (Museum of Indian Arts and Culture) [5] Texas Department of Transportation

05

Removal and the Tribe’s own commemoration

The Tribe dates removal from Fort Griffin to October 1884 and describes travel through the Sac and Fox and Ponca agencies before arrival at Oakland on June 30, 1885. It calls this forced journey its “Trail of Tears” and connects the date with its annual powwow. TxDOT’s later government chronology adds federal-policy context. The Tribe’s commemorative language is presented in its own voice; details are not extended beyond the sources.

Read the sources [1] Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma [5] Texas Department of Transportation

06

The 1891 land cession in two records

A 1892 federal Senate document transmits the 1891 agreement and reproduces agency and commission reports about allotments, the land involved, compensation, and the commissioners’ view of Tonkawa title. A memorial adopted by the Tonkawa Tribe in council in 1907 and presented to Congress in 1908 challenges the agreement’s terms and describes members’ understandings and absences. The memorial and affidavits are primary evidence of the Tribe’s later claim and testimony, not a judicial ruling; the federal reports are evidence of government reasoning, not a neutral account of consent. Reading both makes the disagreement visible without deciding it. Individual allotment schedules and burial-location details are not reproduced.

Read the sources [10] United States Congress, Senate, Congressional Serial Set [12] Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma; printed by the U.S. Senate in the Congressional Serial Set

07

What remains uncertain

Historical sources disagree about the timing and direction of Tonkawa movement, which named bands became associated with the Tonkawa, and possible archaeological links. The proposed Toyah connection in Jones is explicitly uncertain. Secondary accounts give differing casualty estimates for the 1862 massacre; underlying records and community accounts need more direct comparison. A 1996 Handbook entry’s statement that the Tonkawa were no longer distinguishable as a tribe is contradicted by the present-day Tonkawa Tribe and is not used to describe current identity.

Read the sources [5] Texas Department of Transportation [6] Smithsonian Institution, Smithsonian Contributions to Anthropology 2(5) [8] Texas State Historical Association [4] Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma [12] Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma; printed by the U.S. Senate in the Congressional Serial Set

08

Reading path and remaining work

Start with the Tribe’s own history and government pages, then read its public language-learning outline. Compare the 1837 treaty text and 1891 federal agreement record with the council-adopted 1907 memorial, noting the different authors and purposes. TxDOT’s chronology and Jones’s Smithsonian study offer historical syntheses whose cited records and assumptions should be checked. This remains an initial source guide rather than a full history or a community-reviewed account. The documentary is a lead for future work; the film and its interviews were not viewed.

Review completed 2026-10-23. Seven works count toward the substantive inspected-source target; six supporting references are excluded. The source cards state the actual inspected scope, authorship/perspective, review date, and access limits. The 1837 treaty records terms negotiated with the Republic of Texas; it does not prove implementation. The 1891 federal Senate document records agency and commission positions. The 1907 Tonkawa memorial and affidavits are direct evidence of the later community claim and named testimony, not a legal finding. The two land-cession perspectives are cited together. The Tribe’s history and language pages are community-government publications. Older stereotyping and any page descriptions that the Tribe’s site itself identifies as secret are not reproduced. TxDOT describes its statewide Tribal Histories project as collaborative; the individual Tonkawa report does not name a specific Tonkawa reviewer. Jones’s Smithsonian work is a dated scholarly publication based on historical records and museum objects. The archaeology and broad historical classifications are not treated as settled. No undated population or enrollment figure is stated as current. The individual allotment schedules and burial location in the federal records are not copied into the narrative. The owner-supplied Jumano-study URLs remain in the distinct reading-lead catalogue and are not treated as Tonkawa research or completed content checks. No map was inspected or added.

Indigenous-led / community historyTonkawa Tribe of OklahomaSource 1

History | Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma ↗

The Tribe’s own public account identifies its self-name as Tickanwa-tic and describes the 1884–1885 removal from Fort Griffin to Oakland, which the Tribe calls its “Trail of Tears.” It also gives a short account of earlier Texas history and connects the June powwow date to the removal commemoration. The page is undated and contains older stereotypes and generalized language; this guide avoids those passages and attributes its historical account to the Tribe.

Inspection scope: Read the complete visible page body, including the Tribe’s naming statement, brief early-history account, removal sequence, and commemorative framing (page lines 17–46). No linked images or map were inspected.

Tonkawa: They All Stay Together — production and film information ↗

The filmmakers describe a four-year project made in collaboration with the Tonkawa Tribe and say tribal leaders and elders reviewed footage. This statement is the production company’s account of its process, not independent verification. The full film and trailer have not been viewed, so their contents are not used as evidence and this card remains outside the substantive count. The project is a promising lead for future review of public oral-history and contemporary community material; do not assume that all filmed ceremonies are intended for unrestricted circulation.

Inspection scope: Read the complete public project/about pages (turns 2211view3 and 2217view1; visible text lines 5–42 and 7–42 respectively). The trailer, feature film, footage, interviews, and oral histories were not played or read.

Government historical synthesisTexas Department of TransportationSource 5

Tonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma Research Report — TxDOT Tribal Histories ↗

This 30-page chronological research report compiles scholarship and records for Texas transportation planning and public education. TxDOT describes its broader Tribal Histories project as collaborative with participating Tribes, but the Tonkawa report itself does not identify a specific Tribal reviewer or approval; it is therefore treated as a government synthesis, not as a Tonkawa-authored account. Its reconstructions of early bands, locations, and 1862 casualty totals remain attributed to the report and cited literature.

Inspection scope: Read the report introduction and selected chronology: PDF pages 3–10, 15–29, including bibliography entries at pages 29–30. Pages 11–14 and most bibliography entries were not reviewed. Figures/maps were not visually inspected and are not used as map evidence.

Notes on the History and Material Culture of the Tonkawa Indians ↗

Jones places a historical sketch alongside a study of objects collected by U.S. Army surgeon Henry McElderry at Fort Griffin in 1868. The work is valuable for its named documents and the history of the collection, but it reflects a 1969 museum and ethnological framework and relies on older colonial and scholarly accounts. Its proposed archaeological links and broad identity/language classifications are uncertain or dated and are not treated as settled evidence. Object descriptions and images are not reproduced here.

Inspection scope: Read the title/contents, introduction, selected historical-sketch pages (printed pp. 65–71), the conclusion section (printed p. 77), and selected bibliography/context passages. The full object catalogue on printed pp. 74–76 was not reviewed; maps listed by the work were not inspected as images.

Indigenous-led language-learning resource prepared for the TribeTonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma, Language Restoration and Preservation Program SeriesSource 7

Beginning to Learn Tonkawa: An Elementary Outline of Tonkawa Grammar ↗

Paterson prepared this 24-page learning outline for the Tonkawa Tribe’s language-restoration and preservation program. Its introduction describes an educational goal of renewed use and bilingual community life, and the text includes a pronunciation guide, teaching guidance, and a first lesson. This is a language-learning resource, not a substitute for a current account of community language programs; the instructor guidance should be understood in its stated classroom context.

Inspection scope: Read the cover and introduction, pronunciation guide, teaching goals/methods, and the first lesson’s question-and-answer material (PDF pages 1–15 and 18–22). Remaining pages and any associated audio were not reviewed.

Tonkawa Indians — Handbook of Texas Online ↗

A concise older synthesis that can be compared with the Tribe’s account, TxDOT’s 2021 report, and Jones’s 1969 study. The article includes unsourced or broad claims, dated cultural generalizations, and a 1951 statement implying the Tonkawa were no longer a distinct tribe; that last claim conflicts with the contemporary Tonkawa Tribe government and must not be repeated as a fact about present-day identity. Kept as a contextual reference, not counted toward the substantive target.

Inspection scope: Read the complete visible article body and its “Learn More” bibliography (lines 6–47). No linked books or underlying works were read as part of this review.

Agreement with the Tonkawa Tribe for cession of lands in Oklahoma Territory — S. Ex. Doc. 52-13 ↗

This federal document transmits the 1891 Tonkawa land agreement and reproduces reports from the Department of the Interior and the Cherokee Commission. It states aggregate acreage and compensation and records the commissioners’ own description of the transaction and their view of Tonkawa land rights. It is strong evidence of the government’s position and the document sent to Congress, not a neutral account of the negotiation or proof that Tonkawa participants shared the commissioners’ understanding. The individual allotment schedule and burial-location details are not reproduced in this guide.

Inspection scope: Read the full 16-page public PDF’s transmittal, agency/commission reports, agreement articles, and selected contextual pages (PDF pages 1–6). The individualized land schedule was not reviewed in detail or reproduced; the Senate document is a government record of the agreement, not an independent account of consent or implementation.

Primary treaty text in a scholarly archival compilationTexas State Library and Archives Commission / Texas History Trust digital editionSource 11

1837 Treaty between Texas and the Tonkawa — Indian Papers of Texas and the Southwest, vol. I, pp. 28–29 ↗

This transcribed treaty records an agreement between Tonkawa head chiefs and the Republic of Texas. Its articles describe reciprocal promises of peace and a state-appointed trading agent with a controlling role in trade. The document captures the contracting governments’ written terms and the language of its period; it does not establish how each provision worked in practice or provide a complete account of Tonkawa political decision-making. The digitized pages are part of an edited compilation of Texas Indian papers.

Inspection scope: Read the complete treaty transcription across printed pp. 28–29 (digital pages 34–35), including the articles, signatures/marks, and ratification note. The surrounding volume is not counted as read.

Primary community petition and member testimony in a congressional recordTonkawa Tribe of Oklahoma; printed by the U.S. Senate in the Congressional Serial SetSource 12

Memorial of the Tonkawa Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma relating to claims against the United States — S. Doc. 60-206 ↗

This six-page Senate document reproduces a memorial adopted by the Tonkawa Tribe in council and affidavits from members contesting the 1891 cession’s terms and the way it was negotiated. Their claims are direct evidence of the Tribe’s later position and named members’ recollections, not a judicial finding or independent valuation. The memorial’s account should be read alongside the 1892 federal document, which records commissioners’ contrasting assessment. It also reprints older federal agent reports with their own colonial and comparative framing; those passages are attributed rather than adopted.

Inspection scope: Read all six PDF pages, including the council memorial, affidavits by Frank E. Mason, John Rush Buffalo, and John Allen, and appended excerpts from federal agents’ reports. Claims about the negotiation are attributed to the memorialists and affiants; the appended agent language is not treated as Tonkawa testimony. No individualized allotment or burial site details were published.
